source.title: Leveraging Unlabeled Data to Track Memorization
source.authors: Mahsa Forouzesh; Hanie Sedghi; Patrick Thiran

page_placements.theme: Prior training changes subsequent memorization and transfer

record.tranche_reason: Tests how pre-trained models and a theoretical two-layer network converge on randomly labeled data, using a single mislabeled sample or objective loss rather than the original full-set fitting procedure.
record.gate_note: The study tests resistance to fitting a held-out randomly labeled set and how that resistance changes with training-set label noise. It does not report full-set zero-error fitting on wholly random labels, chance test error, shuffled or Gaussian inputs, or regularization effects on fitting random labels. Cited findings about learning before memorization are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study uses random-label fitting to construct a memorization metric. Its step-count experiments compare models with different pretraining histories on a subsequently relabeled sample; its theory compares their subsequent fitting of independently randomized labels. Neither measures V2's training-time comparison between true and corrupted labelings from the same initialization. The supplied text does not establish another claim version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete: the authors conclude that high-test-accuracy models resist subsequent random-label memorization, propose susceptibility to track training-set noise memorization, and combine it with training accuracy for model selection without ground-truth labels.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a held-out randomly labeled set, single-sample continuation experiments, and a theoretical convergence analysis; it does not reproduce full-set training on completely random labels. The proposed susceptibility metric is used to track memorization during noisy-label training.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported single-sample memorization time differs between clean-label and 50%-noise pre-trained GoogLeNet models. The theoretical result varies with original label-noise level and further fitting steps.

fits_no_version.finding: Clean-pretrained GoogLeNet takes 99 steps to memorize an incorrectly relabeled example, versus 2 steps after 50%-noise pretraining.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prior training and resulting generalization performance affect resistance to subsequently memorizing an incorrect label.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report lower subsequent random-label objective values after noisier initial training, supported by an NTK approximation and numerical evaluations of bound terms.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models previously trained with more label noise are more susceptible to fitting a new independent random labeling of the same inputs.

record.problems: The direct step-count comparison is limited to two pre-trained GoogLeNet models and one incorrectly labeled sample. The theoretical convergence result concerns a two-layer ReLU network and objective loss; it does not quantify the claimed small constant-factor time cost for fitting full random-label datasets.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for V2 were omitted. Other susceptibility, model-selection, and test-accuracy results do not measure the fitting-time behavior named by V2; cited prior-work results were excluded.

untested.parts: Full randomly labeled training-set fitting by standard deep networks, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
The constant-factor training-time comparison between true and random labels, and convergence slowing as corruption of the fitted dataset increases.
Zero-error fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
A corruption sweep establishing perfect training fit throughout and steadily worsening test error toward chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them alone impairs true-label generalization.

A demonstrated temporal ordering of shared-pattern learning before noise memorization. The paper records noisy-subset trajectories, but the supplied textual descriptions do not establish this ordering against clean-subset learning.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both proposed V2 supports labels. Faster subsequent memorization after noisier pretraining neither supports nor challenges V2's corruption-dependent convergence claim because the experimental comparison differs.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test standard networks trained from scratch on a completely random labeling of the full training set, zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, or unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.

Tests whether more label noise in the original training data corresponds to faster fitting of held-out random labels, but does not establish the claimed small constant-factor training-time cost or directly compare full-set random-label training time with true-label training time.
Does not test shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Does not test a sweep from zero to all corrupted labels showing perfect training fit at every level and steadily rising test error.
Includes regularized training settings in other analyses, but does not test whether regularization prevents fitting random labels or whether removing it harms true-label generalization.
Learning-before-memorization is discussed with citations to prior work; this study does not test the temporal order of learning real patterns and memorizing random labels.

rows.note: The authors state this lower-test-accuracy network memorizes the new sample after only 2 steps.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network with ReLU non-linearity
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical convergence analysis evaluates objective loss on a held-out randomly labeled set after training on data at varying label-noise levels.
rows.measure: Objective function on held-out randomly labeled set after k training steps and k̃ further steps
rows.value: Authors state Φ̃(k + k̃) decreases as LNL increases and as k̃ increases
rows.uncertainty: Theorem 2: probability at least 1 − δ, given approximation in Equation (4)
rows.note: The result indicates that models trained with higher label-noise levels fit the held-out random labels more readily; it does not report a constant-factor training-time comparison.
rows.check: The comparison varies original training-label noise while keeping the subsequent target labeling independently random. It does not test V2. The theoretical inputs are the original training inputs, not independent held-out inputs. Also, Theorem 2 supplies bounds conditional on Equation (4); their monotonicity with label noise is numerically evaluated, and decreasing bounds alone do not prove monotonicity of every realized objective.

relation.reason: Random-label memorization supplies an evaluation tool; the study does not establish full-set fitting under V1 or compare random-label versus true-label training time under V2.

tranche.reason: Uses subsequent random-label fitting to develop and evaluate a memorization metric. The continuation experiments and convergence analysis measure resistance after different pretraining histories, rather than any claim version's specified comparison.

source_check.notes: R3's evaluation set reuses the original training inputs with independently randomized labels. The authors' monotonicity conclusion combines an objective approximation with numerically observed behavior of the bounds; the conclusion paraphrase is faithful.

reader_labels.condition: Theoretical two-layer ReLU network under the paper’s stated convergence-analysis assumptions
reader_labels.reason: Objective loss on held-out random labels is stated to decrease with higher original label-noise level and with additional fitting steps (R3), supporting the convergence-slowing-with-more-corruption component.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The 50%-noise pre-trained model memorized the incorrect sample in 2 steps, while the clean pre-trained model took 99 steps (R1–R2); this supports faster random-label fitting after noisier training, within this narrow setup.
